name: Irkalla: Gilgamesh's Dream (Arabic: Irkala, Hilm Gilgamesh)
date: 2025. World premiere in the Piazza Grande section of the 78th Locarno Film Festival, August 2025; then Toronto (TIFF, September 2025) and the Red Sea International Film Festival (Arab premiere, December 2025). Iraqi premiere at Al-Jadiriya Mall cinema, Baghdad, 8 February 2026, with Iraqi theatrical release from Eid al-Fitr 2026. Later festival dates include SXSW London 2026 and FESCAAAL 2026 (Milan), where it won the Premio ACEC.
creator: Directed and produced by Mohamed Jabarah Al-Daradji (Iraqi, trained in Hilversum and at the Northern Film School, Leeds). Screenplay credited on Wikipedia to Al-Daradji and Karim Traidia; one Arabic source credits Hassan Falah [uncertain]. Produced by Al-Daradji's Iraqi Independent Film Center with Image Nation Abu Dhabi and Human Film, co-produced by Lionceau Films and Biet Ameen (Iraq, UAE, France, Qatar, UK, Saudi Arabia). Hand-drawn animated sequences by Darvideo Animation Studio (Ukraine, led by Yuriy Polyashko). World sales: MPM Premium.
form: Arabic-language feature film (fiction, roughly 107 to 109 minutes [uncertain]) mixing social-realist drama shot with non-professional child actors, real 2019 protest footage and hand-drawn animated sequences retelling the Gilgamesh myth.
translator_access: Not a translation. Al-Daradji adapts the myth as a filmmaker and Iraqi, drawing on the epic's cultural presence in Iraq rather than on any philological reading of Akkadian. No evidence found of a scholarly crib or a specific English or Arabic translation used [uncertain].
scholarly_adviser: None named in any source found [uncertain].
versions_used: Draws on the popular outline of the epic: Gilgamesh losing his friend Enkidu and journeying to reach the underworld, Irkalla, to bring him back. The film merges the Standard Babylonian quest for life with the underworld material more associated with the Sumerian 'Gilgamesh, Enkidu and the Netherworld' and Tablet XII, which is where Irkalla, as the land of the dead, is most prominent [uncertain]. It also brings in wider Mesopotamian imagery, notably a lamassu (winged bull) walking through modern Baghdad.
non_standard_material: Not applicable in the textual sense. The film silently fuses epic episodes with other Mesopotamian iconography (the lamassu) and with a new plot about orphans in 2019 Baghdad. The myth is marked off formally by switching to hand-drawn animation, framed as a cartoon series about Gilgamesh and Irkalla that the teacher Maryam shows in her bus school (one review says a VHS tape given to Chum-Chum).
gap_policy: Smoothed over. The film uses the myth as a clean, whole story that a child can believe in; lacunae in the tablets are not acknowledged.
typography_of_absence: Nothing on screen marks the gaps in the ancient text. Absence is instead carried by the plot: the missing parents, bodies thrown into the Tigris, a mute child, and a fragmented, disorienting editing style that one critic reads as a sign that 'narrative coherence is no longer possible' (Martin Kudlac, ScreenAnarchy).
tablet_xii: Not addressed as a textual question. Its themes (descent to the underworld, trying to recover the lost dead) are effectively the core of the film, since Chum-Chum believes a gate in the Tigris leads to Irkalla where he can find and revive his parents [uncertain].
turning_point: The hinge is the loss of the companion and the resolve to go down to the underworld to bring him back: Al-Daradji summarises the epic as 'a king who goes on a journey to find his friend who has been killed, to reach Irkalla, the underworld' (ScreenAnarchy interview, 2025). In the film this maps onto Chum-Chum's parents, killed by ISIS and thrown into the Tigris, and his belief that the river holds the gate to Irkalla. Critics also read a parallel in 13-year-old Moody, who roams the city with street children and faces militia recruitment, as a Gilgamesh figure searching for a lost companion (Panos Kotzathanasis, Asian Movie Pulse). The Utnapishtim, Siduri, snake and walls-of-Uruk episodes are not reported as structural hinges in any review found.
arc_interpretation: Grief and the refusal of death, reframed as a national condition. The epic becomes a child's coping story: a nine-year-old diabetic orphan uses the myth as 'a framework for belief' to imagine his dead parents can be recovered (Paul Emmanuel Enicola, The Movie Buff). The underworld is relocated to Baghdad itself: 'the underworld is not a distant realm but the city itself' (Kudlac, ScreenAnarchy). Al-Daradji frames it as a post-ISIS question: 'What happens to a city when it's liberated but the people still don't understand what happened?' The ending, per reviewers, avoids catharsis; the arc reads less as maturity or wisdom than as imagination used as a shield against unbearable loss, and as a diagnosis of Iraq's 'lost generation'. Myth, in the director's words, 'helps us understand who we are.'
key_passages: No fixed-passage renderings. The film does not stage Shamhat and Enkidu, Siduri's advice, the Tablet XI bedchamber scene or the closing walls of Uruk in any source found [uncertain]. The mythic content is carried by animated interludes about Gilgamesh and Irkalla shown in Maryam's mobile classroom, and by a lamassu appearing in present-day Baghdad. The Tigris stands in for the waters of death, described by one critic as 'a living archive of the city's history and memory' (Asian Movie Pulse).
diction_and_metre: Not verse. Contemporary Iraqi Arabic dialogue spoken by non-professional children cast from orphanages, set against hand-drawn animation for the mythic register. Critics describe a mix of documentary realism, 'post-apocalyptic aesthetics and social realism' (Kudlac) and kinetic protest footage; real 2019 Tishreen protest scenes were intercut with staged ones.
sample_line: "Gilgamesh is about a king who goes on a journey to find his friend who has been killed, to reach Irkalla, the underworld. Chum-Chum also has this hope, to go to Irkalla to bring back his family." (Mohamed Al-Daradji, ScreenAnarchy interview, Locarno 2025). From the film itself, as quoted by Asian Movie Pulse: "I dreamt I was in Holland and Chum-Chum had recovered and was having fun."
critical_response: Broadly positive. ScreenAnarchy (Martin Kudlac): 'The film shifts fluidly between intimate character study, societal critique, and kinetic urgency... a sobering commentary on Iraq's lost generation.' Asian Movie Pulse (Panos Kotzathanasis, March 2026): 'an excellent work' showing Iraqi cinema's promising trajectory; the animated segments 'well integrated... providing brief relief from the bleakness.' The Movie Buff (Paul Emmanuel Enicola, TIFF 2025, grade B): 'a necessary, albeit uneasy, watch'; for viewers who do not know the epic 'the mythological layer can feel murky, even distracting', and the supernatural elements risk overshadowing human stakes that need no embellishment. Cineuropa also reviewed it (not accessible). Won the Premio ACEC at FESCAAAL 2026.
controversies: No disputes found over accuracy or authorship. The main critical reservation is whether the myth layer clarifies or muddies the realist story (The Movie Buff). Minor inconsistency across sources in writing credit (Karim Traidia vs Hassan Falah) and runtime (107 vs 109 minutes) [uncertain]. Ethical interest rather than controversy: children cast from real orphanages, and filming inside live 2019 protests, sometimes managing one shot a day.
regional_reception: A direct return of the epic to its region of origin: an Iraqi director, Baghdad setting, Iraqi orphan cast and Arabic dialogue. Arab premiere at Red Sea IFF (Saudi Arabia); also shown at Doha Film. Baghdad premiere on 8 February 2026 at Al-Jadiriya Mall cinema filled the house; Iraqi artist Hafiz Laaibi called it 'a significant work and transformation in cinema', and others hoped it would revive Iraqi box office (964media). Iraqi theatrical release from Eid al-Fitr 2026. Covered in Arabic press (Asharq Al-Awsat, Sayidaty, Al-Muraqeb Al-Iraqi), where Al-Daradji said the project had been growing for 15 years before writing began in 2019.
ai_craft_tension: The film is a strong counterweight to machine-assisted recovery of the epic. Its authority does not come from the text at all: no adviser, no tablets, no fidelity to lines. It comes from lived experience, nearly two decades of the director working with war-orphaned children, a cast drawn from orphanages, and real protest footage captured over 45 difficult days. What a human contributes here is the one thing a corpus cannot supply: deciding what the story is for in Baghdad in 2019, turning the search for Enkidu into a child's search for parents dumped in the Tigris. Even the myth itself is rendered by hand-drawn animation rather than generated imagery. For an essay, it shows the far end of the spectrum: when the epic goes home, it is valued as a living story that helps people 'understand who we are', not as a recovered artefact.
essay_hooks: 1) The epic comes home as a children's cartoon inside the film, shown in a double-decker bus turned mobile school (ScreenAnarchy review; Darvideo). 2) Al-Daradji: 'Myth helps us understand who we are' (ScreenAnarchy interview, 2025). 3) The Tigris as the gate to Irkalla, where ISIS threw the bodies of the boy's parents: the waters of death made literal. 4) 'The underworld is not a distant realm but the city itself' (Kudlac, ScreenAnarchy). 5) Numbers: 150 child actors, 109 shooting days, a 15-year gestation, sometimes one shot a day during real 2019 protests (964media; ScreenAnarchy interview). 6) A full house in Baghdad on 8 February 2026 (964media), a contrast with the museum and database afterlife of the tablets. 7) Counterpoint: to outsiders 'the mythological layer can feel murky, even distracting' (The Movie Buff), a reminder that the epic reads differently at home and abroad.
